title: Choosing a concurrency mechanism
points: First ask whether there is shared, mutable state; if not, no synchronization is needed.
If you protect a single variable, use an atomic variable.

If you protect multiple variables or an invariant and contention is not a concern (human-triggered, moderate load), use a lock: fine-grained if you can partition by resource, otherwise coarse-grained.
If contention is a concern (machine-triggered, high throughput) and you can partition by thread, use thread confinement.
trade: Order of preference is roughly: no sharing, atomic, coarse lock, fine-grained lock, confinement as complexity and scale grow. Read-write lock is a variant for read-heavy data. The right answer depends on what you protect and the load, not on one tool being best.
test: Walk through the decision for an airline seat booking API used by humans, then for an ingest pipeline of machine events keyed by seat.
answer: Humans: multiple variables, moderate load, so a lock, fine-grained per seat if partitionable. Machine events: high throughput with contention, partition by key, so thread confinement.

questions.question: You protect a single counter shared across threads. What does the decision tree say?
questions.explanation: Single variable leads to atomics. Locks are for multi-variable invariants.

questions.question: Multi-variable invariant, human-triggered moderate load, and you can partition by resource. Which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Contention is not a concern but partitioning by resource is possible, so per-resource locks. Coarse is the answer when you cannot partition.

questions.question: Multi-variable invariant, machine-triggered high throughput, can partition by thread. Which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Contention is a concern and work can be partitioned by thread, so confine data to threads and avoid locks.
